title: The Last Seat
moral: Respect and kindness may cost us a little comfort, but they leave our heart feeling full.

pages.text:
The school bus was extra crowded after the museum trip.

Everyone was tired. Some children hugged their bags like pillows. One child had bought a dinosaur pencil and kept roaring softly with it.

"Please tell your pencil to rest," said Meera.

"It is a tired dinosaur," said Kabir.

At the next stop, an elderly woman climbed into the bus with a cloth bag. There were no empty seats.

Aarush was sitting by the window. It was his favourite seat. From there, he could see shops, trees, bikes, and sometimes dogs that looked like they were late for office.

He looked at the woman.

Then he looked outside.

The bus started moving.

The woman held the seat handle, but the bus shook at every speed breaker.

Aarush felt uncomfortable.

He had been walking all day. His feet hurt. His bag was heavy. He wanted to stay seated.

Across the aisle, Meera saw him looking.

"She seems tired," Meera whispered.

Aarush nodded, but he did not move.

Then the bus stopped suddenly. The woman gripped the handle tightly.

Aarush stood up.

"Aunty, please sit here," he said.

The woman looked at him with surprise. "Are you sure, beta?"

Aarush nodded.

She sat down slowly and placed her cloth bag on her lap.

Aarush stood near the seat. His feet still hurt, but his heart felt quieter now.

After a few minutes, the woman opened her bag and took out a small paper packet.

"My grandson made these at school," she said. "He said I should share if I meet a kind child."

Inside were two tiny coconut sweets.

Aarush smiled and took one.

Kabir leaned over. "Does kindness always come with sweets?"

The woman laughed. "Not always."

Meera said, "But it should."

Everyone smiled.

When Aarush reached his stop, the woman raised her hand.

"May you always find a seat when you need one," she said softly.

Aarush waved goodbye.

That night, his feet were still tired.

But when he remembered the woman's smile, he felt proud.

He had given up a seat.

But somehow, he had carried home something much bigger.
